title: Not yours to finish (Avot 2:16)
hookLine: the work isn't yours to finish, nor are you free to stop
tomorrow: at the end of a book, the whole room says one word. which?

lines: A LIST TAPED TO THE MIRROR.
THE DAY IS SHORT; THE WORK IS GREAT.
cards: Noa's goodbye list is taped to her mirror: coffee with the cast, the lake one more time, return the library books, call the summer camp friends, write Saba a letter. Far more lines than days left.
Last night she nearly tore it down: if I can't finish it, why start? Rabbi Tarfon, in Pirkei Avot, sounds like her list.
The day is short, he says, the work is great, the workers are lazy, the reward is much, and the master of the house is pressing. Urgent, every word.
And then, in the very next saying, the same rabbi turns around: it is not upon you to finish the work. Wait. Why would the man in the biggest hurry say that?

teach.b: Read the whole saying and the puzzle starts to solve itself.
It isn't upon you to finish the work, Tarfon says, and you aren't free to walk away from it either. Two halves, and they need each other.

teach.h: THE WORK IS BIGGER THAN ONE LIFE.
teach.b: The first half takes away a weight nobody can carry: the work is bigger than one life, so finishing was never the measure.
The second half takes away the excuse: since nobody finishes, nobody gets to quit because they can't. Put together, the urgency stops being panic.
The day is short, so do today's part. The work is great, so you'll never be the last one doing it.
Some readers hear in this the whole shape of a Jewish life: the Torah studied and never finished, the world repaired and never done, each generation picking up where the last one put the tools down.
Moses on Nebo didn't finish either. That's the detail to carry from Tarfon: the man who said the day is short also gave everyone permission to leave work undone, as long as they don't leave it.
And Noa's list? The point was never the last line. It's the next one.

how: Rabbi Tarfon's saying in Pirkei Avot, 'it is not upon you to finish the work, nor are you free to desist from it', is quoted in Jewish study and in work for repairing the world.

games.q: what does “not yours to finish” mean?
o: permission to stop when the work gets too hard
work too big for one life, which you still keep doing
a warning to finish everything before the day ends

games.q: Rabbi Tarfon's two sayings — tap the pairs.
p: no quitting because you can't finish

s: Tarfon says that since you can't finish, it's fine to stop
you're not free to desist from it.
the rabbi who said 'the day is short' also said you needn't finish
two sayings side by side in Avot, one after the other.
the saying is about finishing your own to-do list on time
it's about work bigger than one life, like study and repairing the world.

games.q: your friend has been tutoring kids at the library. she's leaving for school and says, i didn't fix anything, so what was the point? what do you say?
o: it was never yours to finish; it's yours to do your part, and pass it on.
you're right; if it isn't finished, it didn't really count.
then stay until every kid is caught up; you can't leave work undone.
games.why: Tarfon: it is not upon you to finish the work, nor are you free to desist from it. your part counts, and the work goes on.

practice: Choose one thing from this path you want to keep doing after the summit: a blessing, a page, a candle, a question. Name the most likely thing that will get in its way.
Then decide, plainly, what you'll do when that happens, and say the plan to yourself once.

wordCard.voice: Not yours to finish: Rabbi Tarfon's saying. The work is too great for one life, and you're not free to stop.

orig.note: Hebrew: it is not upon you to finish the work (Pirkei Avot 2:16).

carryVoice: Your line: keep going, even with the list unfinished and the day short. Ten of fourteen. Onward.

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, the work is great…)
Pirkei Avot 2:16 (it is not upon you to finish the work, nor are you free to desist from it)
